status_summary: As of 2026-10-08 the regulatory change the Mandate asked for is in effect at DOJ and ED. Executive Order 14281 (2025-04-23) told agencies to deprioritize disparate-impact enforcement and told the Attorney General to start repealing or amending agency Title VI rules to the extent they contemplate such liability. DOJ removed disparate-impact provisions from its Title VI rules in a final rule published and effective 2025-12-10, and ED removed the effects-based and affirmative-action provisions of 34 CFR part 100 in a final rule published and effective 2026-07-24, stating that it will not pursue Title VI disparate-impact liability against its funding recipients; both rules were issued without notice and comment, and ED cites the exemption for grants and benefits. ED's rule says DOJ reviewed and approved it under Executive Order 12250, which corresponds to the Mandate's call for the Secretary to work with the Attorney General on the regulation. HHS (2026-07-24) and the National Foundation on the Arts and the Humanities (2026-08-26) published parallel rescissions. ED issued a Dear Colleague letter on pupil discipline and Title VI dated 2026-08-18; Education Week describes it as an ED letter of about 20 pages without the force of law, which says schools should not consider race in discipline except in extraordinary circumstances, that Title VI reaches intentional discrimination and not unintentional disparate impact, and that criticizes the 2014 and Biden-era discipline guidance. The reports found do not describe DOJ as a co-issuer. No joint ED-DOJ enforcement statement, review of pending Title VI cases, review of existing resolution agreements, or action on the 2017 Equity in IDEA regulation was found.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14281 revokes two earlier presidential approvals of DOJ Title VI regulations, directs agencies to deprioritize enforcement of rules that include disparate-impact liability, and directs the Attorney General to start repealing or amending agency Title VI regulations to the extent they contemplate such liability.

Executive Order 14280 (published 2025-04-28) directs the Education Secretary, with the Attorney General, to issue new school discipline guidance on Title VI within 30 days, to act against non-compliant agencies, and to report within 120 days with an inventory of Title VI discipline investigations since 2009.

DOJ publishes a final rule, effective the same day and issued without notice and comment, removing the disparate-effect and affirmative-action provisions from its Title VI regulations at 28 CFR 42.104.

ED announces the rule change; a wire report carried by WTOP says 60 civil rights and education groups criticized it and that the disparate-impact standard has been used most often in school discipline cases.

ED publishes a final rule, effective the same day and issued without notice and comment, removing the effect-based and affirmative-action provisions from its Title VI regulations at 34 CFR part 100 and keeping the intent-based prohibitions.

A law-firm alert expects the ED rule to face court challenges because it was issued without notice and comment, names no pending case, and reads the rule as limiting OCR Title VI enforcement to intentional discrimination and harassment.
ED issues a Dear Colleague letter on pupil discipline and Title VI compliance (title and date taken from the ED document link; the PDF could not be opened).

The Daily Signal, which is published by the Heritage Foundation (the Mandate's publisher), reports that ED issued guidance urging schools not to favor or disfavor students by race in discipline, describes it as reversing Obama-era guidance, does not describe DOJ as a co-issuer, and reports that OCR opened Title VI investigations into districts in Fayetteville, Arkansas and Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The article does not link to the letter.

Education Week reports that the Dear Colleague letter issued 2026-08-18 is about 20 pages, has no force of law, tells schools not to consider race in discipline except in extraordinary circumstances, states that Title VI reaches intentional discrimination and not unintentional disparate impact, and criticizes the 2014 and Biden-era guidance; it does not describe DOJ as a co-signer.

The National Foundation on the Arts and the Humanities publishes a rule removing disparate-impact liability from its Title VI regulations, citing the statutory text, constitutional concerns and Executive Order 14281.
